section.title: The Trial before Pilate
section.sectionRationale: The leaders hand Jesus to Pilate. Judas's remorse ends in despair and death, while Jesus stands silent before the governor. The crowd, stirred up, chooses the guilty Barabbas over the innocent Christ; Pilate washes his hands, and the soldiers mock the King with thorns and a robe.
section.thesis: The innocent King is condemned in the place of the guilty: Judas despairs, Pilate evades responsibility, the crowd calls for blood, and a murderer named Barabbas goes free while Jesus is scourged and mocked, the great exchange at the heart of the gospel enacted before our eyes.
section.frameNote: Five beats: Jesus handed to Pilate; the remorse and death of Judas; Jesus silent before Pilate; the crowd choosing Barabbas and Pilate washing his hands; and the soldiers mocking the King.

units.label: Handed to Pilate, and the end of Judas

verses.text: When morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people conspired against Jesus to put Him to death.
They bound Him, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate the governor.
When Judas, who had betrayed Him, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was filled with {{metamelomai|remorse}} and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders.
“I have sinned by betraying {{athoos|innocent}} blood,” he said. “What is that to us?” they replied. “You bear the responsibility.”
So Judas threw the silver into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself.
The chief priests picked up the pieces of silver and said, “It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money.”
After conferring together, they used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners.
That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel,
and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord had commanded me.”
Meanwhile Jesus stood before the governor, who questioned Him: “Are You the {{basileus|King}} of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied.
And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer.
Then Pilate asked Him, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?”
But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement.

units.label: Barabbas and the washing of hands
units.note: the guilty freed, the innocent condemned

verses.text: Now it was the governor’s custom at the feast to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing.
At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner named Barabbas.
So when the crowd had assembled, Pilate asked them, “Which one do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?”
For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him.
While Pilate was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent him this message: “Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him.”
But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death.
“Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” asked the governor. “Barabbas,” they replied.
“What then should I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate asked. They all answered, “Crucify Him!”
“Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!”

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that instead a riot was breaking out, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. “I am innocent of this man’s blood,” he said. “You bear the responsibility.”
All the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”
So Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.
Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole company around Him.
They stripped Him and put a scarlet robe on Him.
And they twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on His head. They put a staff in His right hand, knelt down before Him, and mocked Him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!”
Then they spit on Him and took the staff and struck Him on the head repeatedly.
After they had mocked Him, they removed the robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him away to crucify Him.

metamelomai.gloss: To feel regret or remorse. Judas is seized with remorse and even confesses, yet it is not the saving repentance (metanoia) that turns to God for mercy; his remorse ends in despair and self-destruction rather than in returning to Christ.

athoos.gloss: Innocent, guiltless. Judas confesses he has betrayed innocent blood, and Pilate declares himself innocent of this man's blood; on every side Jesus' innocence is testified even as He is condemned, the spotless one dying for the guilty.

basileus.gloss: King. Pilate asks if Jesus is the King of the Jews, and the soldiers mock Him as king with thorns and a robe; the deep irony is that He truly is the King, reigning through the very humiliation they intend as scorn.

basic.context: At dawn the leaders deliver Jesus, bound, to Pilate the Roman governor. Judas, horrified at what he has done, returns the money, confesses he betrayed innocent blood, and hangs himself. Before Pilate, Jesus is silent under accusation. Pilate, knowing the leaders act from envy and warned by his wife, tries to release Jesus by the festival custom, but the crowd, stirred up, demands Barabbas, a notorious prisoner, and shouts for Jesus to be crucified. Pilate washes his hands, releases Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock Him as king with thorns and a robe.
basic.hermeneutics: The scene is thick with irony and substitution. Barabbas, a guilty man, goes free because the innocent takes his place, a picture of the gospel. Judas's remorse warns that regret is not repentance. Pilate's hand-washing shows that neutrality is impossible; refusing to do right is doing wrong. Read the mockery knowing that Jesus is in truth the King they ridicule.
basic.originalLanguages: Judas feels metamelomai, remorse, but not saving repentance. Everyone testifies that Jesus is athoos, innocent, even as He is condemned. And Pilate and the soldiers name Him basileus, King, in mockery, while He truly reigns.
basic.typology: Barabbas set free while Jesus is bound pictures the substitution of the cross. Jesus silent before His accusers fulfills the servant of Isaiah 53. The crown of thorns recalls the curse of Genesis 3, now worn by the one who bears the curse for us.
basic.christ: Jesus is the innocent King condemned in the place of the guilty. He stands silent as the servant, is exchanged for a murderer, and wears a crown of thorns, reigning through humiliation. Every mockery unwittingly speaks the truth: this is the King.
basic.god: God's saving plan advances through human sin and evasion; even Pilate's cowardice and the crowd's fury serve the redemption God intends. God testifies to Jesus' innocence through Judas, Pilate, and Pilate's wife, so that the substitution is unmistakably of the guiltless for the guilty.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 gives the silent servant condemned for others. Zechariah 11 gives the thirty pieces and the potter. Psalm 22 lies behind the mockery. Romans 5 declares Christ died for the ungodly, the truth Barabbas pictures.
basic.oneStory: The great exchange is enacted in a courtyard: the guilty Barabbas walks free because the innocent Jesus takes his cross. Judas's despair and Pilate's evasion show that no one can wash their hands of Christ, while the mocking crown proclaims a King reigning through shame. The story drives toward the cross, where the innocent dies for the guilty and the true King is enthroned, so that every Barabbas, every one of us, may go free.

context.literary:
The chapter is stitched from alternating scenes, and the stitching carries the meaning. Matthew 27:1 and 2 hand Jesus to Pilate, then the story swerves to Judas in verses 3 to 10, then returns to Pilate in verse 11 with the word 'Meanwhile.' The two trials run side by side: the council that condemns Jesus will not take back the money it paid to have Him arrested, and the governor who will not condemn Him cannot bring himself to let Him go. Between them stands Judas, whose confession of innocence is the first of five declarations in a row that Jesus is without guilt.

Those declarations are the spine of the chapter. Judas says he betrayed 'innocent blood,' verse 4. Pilate knows the charge is envy, verse 18. His wife calls Him 'that innocent man,' verse 19. Pilate asks what evil He has done and receives no answer, verse 23. Finally Pilate announces his own innocence of 'this man's blood,' verse 24. Everyone testifies to the innocence of the one they hand over.

Matthew also plays with the word for 'handed over.' The leaders hand Jesus to Pilate in verse 2, Pilate hands Him to be crucified in verse 26, and the verb is the one used for Judas' betrayal throughout the Gospel. Handing over passes from hand to hand until it reaches the cross.

The mock coronation in verses 27 to 31 balances the earlier question 'Are You the King of the Jews?' in verse 11. In verse 11 the title is a charge; in verse 29 it is a joke; in verse 37 it will be a sign over the cross. The title is true each time, and the one who speaks it never realises.

Matthew alone gives us Pilate's wife, the handwashing and the crowd's cry, the scenes that sharpen the chapter's moral questions: who is responsible, and can anyone keep their hands clean?
context.historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36 as prefect, a Roman equestrian officer with command of troops and the power of life and death. A limestone block from the theatre at Caesarea, discovered in 1961, names him with that title, and the Roman historian Tacitus records that Christ was executed under Pilate in the reign of Tiberius. Matthew calls him simply 'the governor.' His seat was at Caesarea, but he came up to Jerusalem at the great feasts, when the city swelled with pilgrims and nationalist tempers ran hot, and he sat in judgment before the Praetorium or governor's residence.

The Jewish council had no authority to carry out a death sentence, John 18:31, so it needed Pilate to do the killing. Its charge before him was political, 'proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King,' as Luke records in Luke 23:2, since a claim to kingship was a crime against Caesar. John 19:12 shows the pressure that finally bent Pilate: 'you are no friend of Caesar.'

The Passover custom of releasing a prisoner is mentioned in the Gospels but is not independently attested in other ancient writings. Barabbas, whose name means 'son of the father' in Aramaic, is called a notorious prisoner here and an insurrectionist in John 18:40. Some ancient manuscripts of Matthew 27:16 and 17 call him 'Jesus Barabbas,' a reading the BSB footnotes record, which would sharpen Pilate's question: which Jesus, the son of the father who led a revolt or the Son of the Father who was called Christ?

Judas' death is told differently in Acts 1:18 and 19, where the field is bought with his reward and he falls headlong; many readers combine the two accounts, since a hanging body that fell would fit both. The potter's field fits Jeremiah's visit to the potter, Jeremiah 18:2 to 4, and the Valley of Ben-hinnom, filled with innocent blood, Jeremiah 19:4. Roman flogging before crucifixion was brutal, and the soldiers' mock robe and crown parodied the dress of an emperor.
context.canonical:
Matthew quotes a prophecy in verses 9 and 10 and names Jeremiah, but the wording comes from Zechariah 11:12 and 13, 'thirty pieces of silver' thrown 'to the potter in the house of the LORD.' Matthew combines it with Jeremiah's own scenes at the potter's house and the field he bought, Jeremiah 18:2 to 4, 19:1 to 4 and 32:6 to 9. The thirty pieces recall the price of an injured slave, Exodus 21:32, so the shepherd's wages in Zechariah are an insult, and Matthew shows the insult fulfilled in Judas.

Judas' death also echoes David's counsellor Ahithophel, who went home and hanged himself after turning against the king, 2 Samuel 17:23, and the psalm Jesus quoted of Judas, 'the one who shared My bread has lifted up his heel against Me,' Psalm 41:9 with John 13:18.

Pilate's handwashing borrows a Jewish ritual. Deuteronomy 21:6 to 9 required the elders of a town nearest a murdered man to wash their hands and declare, 'Our hands did not shed this blood,' and Psalm 26:6 speaks of washing the hands in innocence. A Roman governor performs a Jewish act of disclaiming blood, and it condemns him. The crowd's answer, 'His blood be on us,' echoes Jewish phrases for taking responsibility for a death, and it invites the later verdict of Hebrews 12:24 that Jesus' sprinkled blood 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.'

The suffering of verses 26 to 31 is the pattern of the servant, silent before accusers, Isaiah 53:7, giving His back to the strikers and His face to spittle, Isaiah 50:6, disfigured beyond that of any man, Isaiah 52:14. The New Testament comments on the trial in Acts 4:27 and 28, in 1 Timothy 6:13 and in 1 Peter 2:23, 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' while Psalm 2:2 had foretold rulers gathering against the Lord's Anointed.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers to hear the verdict of innocence from every mouth that could be heard, and to see that the sentence came anyway. The point is not that the system malfunctioned. It is that Jesus died as the righteous for the unrighteous, as the Gospel will go on to say, and this had to happen with the truth about His innocence on public record so that no one could say He deserved it.

He also gives three portraits of failure for his readers to weigh. Judas feels the weight of guilt and takes his own life; he carries the sin to men who will not relieve him and not to God. The leaders keep scrupulous rules about blood money while shedding innocent blood. Pilate recognises the truth and surrenders it under pressure. In each case a person has the truth and still does the wrong thing, and Matthew wants his readers to see that knowing is not enough.

He closes the scene with the soldiers' mockery so that the reader hears the ironic truth in each insult. The crown, the robe and the reed are the trappings of a king, and the cry 'Hail, King of the Jews!' is exactly what the readers of the Gospel should say with sincerity. Matthew's audience, many of them Jewish, are asked to hear in the mockery the confession they are meant to make.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter records sin; it does not recommend it. Judas' suicide is reported as a tragedy and never commended, and the leaders' scruples over blood money are shown as hypocrisy. Pilate's handwashing is a gesture that fails. No one reading Matthew can conclude that washing hands, paying off a debt of conscience, or saying 'you bear the responsibility' removes guilt.

The cry of verse 25, 'His blood be on us and on our children!', is a description of what a crowd said, and not a statement of God's will or a curse He placed on a people. Matthew does not say God accepted it, and the same Gospel records Jesus asking forgiveness, in Luke 23:34, for those who put Him to death. Reading it as a license for contempt toward Jewish people has been a grave misuse of the text, and the apostles, all Jews, preached the gospel to their own people in hope, Acts 3:17 to 19.

What does carry forward is the lesson of the contrasts. Remorse must lead to repentance and to the one who forgives, not to despair. Neutrality before Jesus is a decision. And the believer is invited to take up the confession the soldiers mock, that He is King, and to follow the Servant who answered abuse without retaliation, 1 Peter 2:23.

debates.question: How should 'His blood be on us and on our children' in verse 25 be understood?

views.label: A rhetorical cry of a Jerusalem crowd, not a doctrine of collective guilt
views.case: The speakers are those present, 'all the people' of verse 25 in the sense of the crowd gathered before Pilate, and the phrase is a way of saying they would accept responsibility. Peter later tells the same city that they acted in ignorance and calls them to repent, Acts 3:17 to 19, so the cry does not close the door on mercy.

views.label: A prophetic sign of the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70
views.case: Some readers connect the cry with Jesus' warnings about that generation, Matthew 23:35 to 36 and 24:2, and with the destruction of the temple. They see a historical consequence for that generation, not an inherited curse on later Jewish people.

views.label: An ironic prayer that becomes a blessing
views.case: Others stress the irony: the blood they invoked is the 'blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28. The crowd asked for the blood to be on them, and the gospel is that it can be, for cleansing.

debates.bearing: On any reading, Matthew does not teach that later generations of Jews are guilty of Jesus' death. Jews and Gentiles together share responsibility, as Acts 4:27 says, and the church has repeatedly condemned using this verse to justify hatred.

debates.question: Why does Matthew attribute the quotation in verses 9 and 10 to Jeremiah?

views.label: A composite quotation named for the greater prophet
views.case: The wording comes mainly from Zechariah 11:12 and 13, but the potter and the purchased field are Jeremiah's scenes, Jeremiah 18, 19 and 32. Ancient writers sometimes named only the more prominent prophet when blending two texts, as Mark does with Malachi and Isaiah in Mark 1:2 and 3.

views.label: A scribal slip in an early copy
views.case: Others suggest the name was added or garbled in transmission. A few manuscripts and versions do substitute Zechariah or leave the name out, but that looks more like an attempt to smooth the difficulty than the original reading.

views.label: Jeremiah as the prophet of the broken pot and the new covenant
views.case: Some say the allusion is to the whole Jeremiah theme of judgment on a city filled with innocent blood, with the potter's field as its sign, so the fulfilment is thematic and not just verbal.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Matthew sees the buying of the potter's field as the working out of what the prophets had already pictured. The main teaching is not affected by the question of the name: the betrayal price, the temple and the potter are all in Scripture beforehand.

debates.question: What does Judas' remorse show?

views.label: He was a lost man who only felt regret
views.case: Judas confesses sin but turns to the priests and not to God, and the narrative does not suggest forgiveness. Jesus had said it would be better for that man not to have been born, Matthew 26:24.

views.label: His end warns of the limits of conscience
views.case: A guilty conscience can recognise sin and still not know the remedy. The text shows what conscience cannot do and invites the contrast with Peter, who wept and was restored.

views.label: We should not claim to know his final state
views.case: The text does not state it, and some readers prefer to leave the matter in God's hands while accepting the warning the narrative gives.

debates.bearing: The passage clearly teaches that regret differs from repentance, and it leaves questions about Judas' final end to God, to whom judgment belongs.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for Judas' feeling in verse 3 is not the usual Greek word for repentance. Matthew uses it elsewhere only of a son who first refused his father and 'later changed his mind and went,' Matthew 21:29, and of the leaders who did not 'change their minds afterward' to believe John, Matthew 21:32. The word describes a change of heart that may or may not lead to a changed direction. What distinguishes Judas is not the feeling but where it carries him: back to the men who hired him, not to the Lord he betrayed. The verb Matthew uses for real repentance throughout the Gospel is a different one, as in Matthew 3:2 and 4:17.

The key verb for the whole chapter is 'handed over,' which Matthew uses of Judas' betrayal, of the leaders delivering Jesus to Pilate in verse 2, of Pilate handing Him over in verse 26. It is also the verb of the Greek version of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant 'was handed over' for the sins of many. Every human hand that passes Jesus along is also, in the larger plan, a hand of the Father giving up His Son, as Romans 8:32 says. The word 'envy' in verse 18 names the motive Pilate saw: the leaders were moved less by principle than by jealous rivalry.

In verse 19 Pilate sits on the 'judgment seat,' a raised platform that was the symbol of Roman justice. The scene is the most grotesque image of justice in the Gospel: the judge sits where justice should be done, and a message about an innocent man's dream arrives, and he does nothing. In verse 24 Pilate 'washed his hands' with a verb that means to wipe or rinse off, a gesture that Matthew alone records.

'Flogged' in verse 26 comes from a Latin loan word, flagellum, as does the word for the Praetorium and the 'company' of soldiers, so Matthew's Greek preserves the sound of the occupying army. The mock robe is a scarlet cloak, the soldier's colour, and the staff in His hand is a reed. 'Hail' in verse 29 is the ordinary Greek greeting, also the word for 'rejoice,' and it echoes the Roman cry 'Ave' offered to the emperor, so the soldiers act out an imperial homage as a joke. 'Struck Him on the head repeatedly' uses a tense of repeated action, a beating that went on.

The Aramaic name Barabbas, 'son of the father,' and the potter's 'field of blood,' which Acts names in Aramaic as Akeldama, show how much of Jerusalem's own speech was woven into the story.

typology.fulfillment: The guilty man walks free because the innocent one is put in his place, and 'son of the father' is exchanged for the Son of the Father. The pattern is substitution, which Scripture elsewhere says outright: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and 'Christ died for us' while we were still sinners, Romans 5:8. The scene is not a deliberate allegory by Barabbas, who simply benefits from the exchange, but it is a living picture of what the cross does for the guilty. The correspondence falls short in one way: Barabbas is freed once, while the cross frees everyone who trusts Him.

typology.type: The potter's field and the thirty pieces
typology.fulfillment: The thirty pieces of silver, the potter and the field are the story of Zechariah 11 and the potter of Jeremiah replayed. The shepherd is valued at the price of a gored slave, Exodus 21:32, and that price is thrown into the house of the LORD. The fulfilment shows that the rejection of the Shepherd-King was foretold, and that the betrayer's money cannot be used for the temple treasury but ends up buying a burial place for strangers. The irony reaches further, because the blood money purchases a field for foreigners, and the gospel will soon reach exactly such people, Matthew 28:19.

Jesus' refusal to answer the charges fits Isaiah 53:7 and the servant who was 'oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth.' Peter reflects on it directly: when abused, He 'did not retaliate,' entrusting Himself to the One who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The escalation is that the servant's silence in Isaiah leads to the justifying of many, Isaiah 53:11. The type does not fully apply to us, since only He bears sin; believers follow His example of non-retaliation, but they do not make atonement.

typology.type: The crown of thorns and the scarlet robe
typology.fulfillment: Thorns are the sign of the curse on the ground, Genesis 3:18, and the soldiers press them onto the head of the one who is about to bear the curse. Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The scarlet robe and the reed sceptre are a parody of royalty, and Isaiah's servant was 'disfigured beyond that of any man,' Isaiah 52:14, yet that same chapter says kings will shut their mouths because of Him, Isaiah 52:15. The thorn link is an inference, not a claim the text makes, but a fitting one.

study.christ:
The evidence for His innocence is stacked deliberately. A betrayer says it, a governor says it, a governor's wife says it, and even the crowd cannot say what evil He has done, verse 23. He is not treated as guilty for any wrong He did; He is treated as guilty for what others did. The apostle puts the exchange plainly: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

He is the King who will not defend His kingship. Asked 'Are You the King of the Jews?' He answers only 'You have said so,' verse 11. In John's account He adds that His kingdom is not of this world and that He came 'to testify to the truth,' John 18:36 and 37, and that Pilate would have no authority unless it were given from above, John 19:11. Here Matthew lets the silence speak. The One who made the governor and the soldiers submits to being judged by them, and from that humiliation He will rise to a throne, as Philippians 2:8 to 11 sets out.

He is the true Shepherd valued at a slave's price. The thirty pieces recall the Shepherd of Zechariah 11, and the money is thrown at the temple. The one betrayed for such a sum is the Shepherd who gave Himself for the flock. He is also the one whose blood, called down by a crowd, is the 'blood of the covenant' that He Himself named at the supper, Matthew 26:28. The cry meant as a curse is turned by Him into the price of forgiveness.

He is the one who takes the curse. The crown of thorns presses a symbol of the fall onto His head, and flogging opens His back. Hebrews and Galatians explain what is happening: He bears the penalty so that those who trust Him are free, Galatians 3:13. The man who is bound in verse 2 is the One who breaks the bonds of everyone else.

The danger in reading this chapter is to find Jesus' meaning in details that Matthew does not draw out. The hand-washing, the dream and the colour of the robe are not coded symbols; they are the true events of the trial. The links to Christ run through the verdicts of innocence, the exchange for Barabbas, the silence of the Servant and the King mocked as King, all of which the New Testament itself picks up.
study.god:
The chapter shows God's hidden sovereignty over a miscarriage of justice. Everyone in it acts freely and wickedly: the priests from envy, Pilate from fear, the crowd from stirred-up passion, the soldiers from cruelty. Yet Matthew has already said that this is happening in fulfilment of the Scriptures, and the church later prays that Herod and Pilate carried out what God's 'hand and will had decided beforehand,' Acts 4:27 and 28. God is not the author of their sin, but He is the author of the salvation that He brings out of it. This is one of the deepest mysteries of the Bible, and the passage lets it stand without explaining it away.

God is the Judge of the innocent blood. The law required the elders of a town near an unsolved killing to wash their hands and ask the LORD not to hold innocent blood against His people, Deuteronomy 21:6 to 9. That law shows how seriously God takes the spilling of innocent blood. Pilate invokes the ritual and then hands the innocent man over anyway, which shows how empty a human declaration of innocence is. In God's court the question is not who washed his hands but who shed the blood.

God is also true to what He has said through the prophets. The thirty pieces, the potter and the field belong to words spoken centuries before, and the way they come together shows that nothing in the story is outside His knowledge. The fulfilment includes even the traitor's money. The God who commands that no innocent blood be shed is the God who, in the cross, provides the one sacrifice that deals with all blood, Hebrews 9:12.

God's holiness and mercy are held together. The chapter has the weight of judgment, as Judas goes to his death and the crowd calls down a curse, yet its end is a King wearing a crown of thorns, a King who in His love bears the curse. The wrath that sin deserves falls on His Son, and the mercy that sinners need flows to them. The God of Matthew 27 is not indifferent to injustice, and He is not a God who answers it only with vengeance.

For worship, the chapter calls us to bow before the Father who gave up His Son, and the Son who gave up Himself. It also invites us to trust that He sees the unjust verdicts we suffer and that He turns them, as He did here, to His purposes. We do not need to wash our hands; we need to be washed.

crossReferences.note: The shepherd is paid thirty pieces of silver, 'this magnificent price,' and told to throw it to the potter in the house of the LORD. Matthew sees this fulfilled when Judas throws the money into the temple and the priests buy the potter's field. The prophecy shows that the rejection was foretold, and that the insult in the price was part of Scripture.

Jeremiah is sent to buy a clay jar and speak against a place that has been filled 'with the blood of the innocent.' Matthew's reference to Jeremiah draws on this scene. Judgment on a city that sheds innocent blood is the backdrop to the purchase of a field with blood money.

Elders wash their hands over a heifer and declare their hands did not shed the blood, asking that innocent blood not be held against Israel. Pilate's handwashing echoes this, and it shows the hollowness of the act: a ritual of atonement performed by one who has not seen the real innocent victim in front of him.

The servant did not open His mouth. In Matthew 27:12 to 14 the Lord stays silent before accusation, even when Pilate asks whether He hears the charges. The silence fits the pattern the prophet saw, and Pilate's amazement shows how unusual it was in a man on trial for his life.

The servant offers his back to those who strike and does not hide his face from scorn and spittle. The soldiers' spitting and beating in Matthew 27:30 line up with the prophet's picture. What looks like random cruelty is the pattern of the one who chose not to turn away.

Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse, as Deuteronomy 21:23 says of one hung on a tree. The thorns, the scourge and the cross are the shape of that curse-bearing. Matthew shows the beginning of it in the soldiers' mockery, and Paul interprets what it meant.

God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that we might become God's righteousness. This is the verse behind Barabbas' release. The guilty goes free and the innocent takes the guilt, and the exchange is not a miscarriage but the heart of the gospel.

The believers read the trial as the meeting of Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel in a gathering that did only what God had already planned. Human guilt and divine purpose coexist, and the passage guards us from using the second to excuse the first.

When abused, Christ made no threats, and entrusted Himself to the one who judges justly. Peter gives the reason for the silence of Matthew 27:12 to 14 and the quiet under the soldiers' blows: the Son handed the case to the Father, and it holds out the same pattern for believers who suffer.

The sprinkled blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel, whose blood cried out for justice, Genesis 4:10. The crowd's cry of Matthew 27:25 is answered by a blood that speaks forgiveness. It is a moving reversal of what the crowd intended.

study.oneStory:
The first murder in Scripture ends with innocent blood crying out from the ground, Genesis 4:10. From that moment the question runs through the story: how can blood that has been shed be answered? The law's answer was substitutes, a heifer for an unsolved killing, lambs and goats at the altar, but none of them could settle the matter, Hebrews 10:4. Matthew 27 shows the question reaching its climax. The blood of the one truly innocent man is shed, and it is the answer and not another accusation.

The chapter also answers Eden. Adam took what he was told not to take, and thorns grew from the ground, Genesis 3:18. Here the second Adam wears the thorns, taking on Himself the curse of the first man's choice. The first man was offered a kingdom to tend and grasped for more. The last Adam is mocked as a king and does not grasp, Philippians 2:6 to 8.

It gathers Israel's story as well. The nation was God's firstborn son, called out of Egypt, Exodus 4:22, and Israel's shepherds had failed again and again, Ezekiel 34. Here the true Shepherd is sold for the price of a slave, and the rulers of the people choose a rebel over their Messiah. Yet in the very rejection, God does what He promised through the prophets, and the Shepherd who is struck is the one who will gather the scattered, as Zechariah 13:7 and Matthew 26:31 and 32 have already said.

Beyond the cross the story moves to the resurrection, which overturns the verdict of Pilate and the priests, and to the commission to all nations, Matthew 28:18 to 20. The potter's field, bought with blood money to bury strangers, is a small sign that the death of Jesus would make a place for outsiders. Paul says that those who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:13.

The story ends in a new creation where there is no curse and no thorn. The King is no longer mocked but worshiped, and the Lamb that was slain is praised for purchasing people from every tribe and nation with His blood, Revelation 5:9 and 10. The crown the soldiers twisted is replaced by many crowns, and the scarlet robe by the righteousness that the redeemed wear, Revelation 19:12 and 13. There the question of Pilate, 'What then should I do with Jesus?', has its last answer, in a crowd that cries not 'Crucify Him!' but 'Worthy.'

quiz.q: What does the release of Barabbas illustrate about the cross?

options.text: The guilty go free because the innocent Jesus takes their place, the substitution at the heart of the gospel.
options.note: Barabbas, a murderer, is freed while the sinless Jesus is condemned, picturing substitution.

options.text: That Pilate found a clever way to release a prisoner at the feast.
options.note: The custom is the setting, but the deeper meaning is the innocent dying for the guilty, which this misses.

options.text: That the crowd made a random choice between two prisoners.
options.note: The choice was stirred up by the leaders and carries the weight of substitution, not randomness.

options.text: That Jesus and Barabbas were equally guilty.
options.note: Jesus is repeatedly declared innocent; Barabbas was the guilty one set free.

quiz.q: How does Judas's remorse differ from true repentance?

options.text: He felt regret and confessed his sin, but despaired and destroyed himself instead of turning to God for mercy.
options.note: Verses 3-5 show remorse without the saving repentance that returns to Christ.

options.text: He felt nothing at all about betraying Jesus.
options.note: He did feel deep remorse; the failure was that it led to despair, not to God, which this denies.

options.text: He repented fully and was restored like Peter.
options.note: Unlike Peter's tears leading to restoration, Judas's remorse ended in despair and death.

options.text: He simply returned the money and moved on with life.
options.note: He was overwhelmed and took his own life, not indifferent.

quiz.q: What does Matthew emphasize about Jesus throughout the trial?

options.text: His innocence, testified by Judas, Pilate, and Pilate's wife, even as He is condemned.
options.note: The repeated declarations of innocence highlight the guiltless dying for the guilty.

options.text: That Jesus defended Himself skillfully against the charges.
options.note: He was largely silent, not mounting a defense; His innocence is testified by others.

options.text: That the charges against Him were basically true.
options.note: The charges were false; He is declared innocent on every side.

options.text: That Pilate found Him guilty after careful investigation.
options.note: Pilate declared Him innocent and yielded to the crowd, not to evidence.

quiz.q: What is the irony in the soldiers' mockery of Jesus as king?

options.text: He truly is the King, reigning through the very humiliation they intend as scorn.
options.note: The crown of thorns and mock homage unwittingly proclaim the real King.

options.text: The soldiers secretly believed He was a king.
options.note: They mocked in unbelief; the irony is that their scorn speaks a truth they did not grasp.

options.text: The mockery had no deeper meaning at all.
options.note: Matthew presents it as heavy with irony, since Jesus is the true King.

options.text: Jesus was only pretending to be a king.
options.note: He is genuinely the King; the mockery ironically declares the truth.

questions: Barabbas walked free because Jesus took his place. How does seeing yourself as the guilty one set free change the way you receive the cross?
Judas felt deep remorse but never turned to Christ for mercy. What is the difference in your own life between merely regretting sin and truly repenting of it?
Pilate tried to wash his hands of a decision he could not avoid. Where are you tempted to think you can stay neutral about Jesus when neutrality is really refusal?
The crowd was stirred up to shout for crucifixion. How can you guard your own convictions from being swept along by the mood of a crowd?
The mocked King was reigning all along. Where do you need to trust that Christ is King even when His way looks like weakness and defeat?

translationNotes.note: The fulfillment quotation blends Zechariah 11:12-13 with imagery from Jeremiah 19 and 32; Matthew attributes it to Jeremiah, the major prophet, a recognized way of citing a composite prophetic text.
Some manuscripts read Jesus Barabbas, sharpening the contrast between Jesus Barabbas and Jesus who is called Christ; the crowd chooses one Jesus over the other.
Some manuscripts read this righteous blood; Pilate's hand-washing echoes Deuteronomy 21 and Psalm 26:6, but the gesture cannot actually remove his responsibility for handing Jesus over.
